title: Phrasal Verbs with On and Off: Continuation, Relationships and Reactions
summary: Use phrasal verbs with on to describe continuation, progress and relationships, and verbs with off to describe falling asleep, completing tasks, alarms, discouragement, cheating, boasting and criticism. Choose the right particle, following pattern and object position.
learningObjectives: Distinguish go on, carry on, keep on and get on according to meaning and grammatical pattern.
Describe progress and interpersonal relationships using get on and get on with.
Use off expressions for sleep, finishing an activity and an alarm sounding.
Express discouragement, unfair treatment, boasting and criticism with put off, rip off, show off and tell off.

explanation.heading: Continue with on: actions and activities
explanation.body: Go on and carry on can mean continue an action rather than stop. Use go on doing or carry on doing with an -ing verb. For a named task, go on with or carry on with + noun is natural. Keep on doing suggests repeated or persistent behaviour; keep doing is also possible. Use walk on or drive on to continue moving.
explanation.example: Even after the lights went out, the pianist carried on playing.

explanation.heading: Get on: progress, relationships and returning to tasks
explanation.body: Get on can describe how an activity or a person is progressing: How are you getting on? Get on with somebody concerns whether people have a good relationship, while get on with a task means continue or resume it. The with phrase is essential when naming the colleague or task.
explanation.example: After the interruption, Nia got on with her presentation.

explanation.heading: Falling asleep, finishing and alarms: off
explanation.body: Doze off, nod off and drop off mean fall asleep, usually without planning to. Finish something off means complete the remaining part of it; a pronoun goes before off (finish it off). An alarm goes off when it sounds, even though off may suggest stopping in other expressions.
explanation.example: The smoke detector went off while we were preparing lunch.

explanation.heading: Discouragement and unfair treatment
explanation.body: Put somebody off an activity means make them less willing to do it. The natural structures are put someone off + noun and put someone off doing something. Rip somebody off means charge unfairly or cheat them; be ripped off describes the person who was cheated. These are not the same as put off an event, which means postpone it.
explanation.example: An unnecessarily complicated form put several applicants off applying.

explanation.heading: Criticism and attracting attention
explanation.body: Show off means behave in a way designed to impress others. Tell somebody off means criticise them angrily for a mistake or bad behaviour, typically tell someone off for doing something. Both are common in conversation, but tell somebody off suggests a stronger rebuke than a calm reminder.
explanation.example: The supervisor told the delivery driver off for ignoring the safety rule.

comparisons.title: Continued activity versus a repeated habit

left.label: carry on + -ing
left.example: Despite the interruption, the band carried on rehearsing.
left.note: The performance of an existing activity continues.

right.label: keep on + -ing
right.example: The phone keeps on ringing during meetings.
right.note: The ringing happens persistently or repeatedly.

left.label: get on with somebody
left.example: Maya gets on with her new housemates.
left.note: This is about having a good relationship.

right.label: get on with something
right.example: Maya must get on with her assignment.
right.note: This is about continuing a task.

comparisons.title: Two different meanings of put off

left.label: put an event off
left.example: They put the workshop off until March.
left.note: The event is postponed to a later date.

right.label: put someone off doing something
right.example: The high fee put them off attending.
right.note: Someone loses the desire to take part.

examples.sentence: When the debate became noisy, the moderator asked everyone to carry on calmly.
examples.note: Carry on means continue, even after a disruption.

examples.sentence: The apprentices are getting on well with their trainers.
examples.note: Get on well with describes a positive relationship.

examples.sentence: Once the power returned, we got on with the experiment.
examples.note: Get on with an activity means resume work on it.

examples.sentence: I nearly nodded off while reading on the late train.
examples.note: Nod off is an unplanned transition into sleep.

examples.sentence: The sudden siren went off just after midnight.
examples.note: An alarm or siren goes off when it makes a sound.

examples.sentence: The seller ripped us off by charging twice the normal price.
examples.note: Rip somebody off means charge them unfairly.

examples.sentence: The coach told the players off for arriving after the warm-up.
examples.note: Tell somebody off for + -ing names the behaviour criticised.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We carried on to discuss the proposal.
commonMistakes.correct: We carried on discussing the proposal.
commonMistakes.why: Carry on meaning continue is followed by an -ing verb, not an infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Jules gets on well his neighbours.
commonMistakes.correct: Jules gets on well with his neighbours.
commonMistakes.why: Get on with somebody needs with to express a relationship.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I must get on my report after lunch.
commonMistakes.correct: I must get on with my report after lunch.
commonMistakes.why: Get on with + task means resume or continue it.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The confusing directions put off me travelling.
commonMistakes.correct: The confusing directions put me off travelling.
commonMistakes.why: With the meaning discourage, put somebody off places the pronoun between the verb and particle.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The manager told off her for leaving early.
commonMistakes.correct: The manager told her off for leaving early.
commonMistakes.why: A pronoun object in separable tell somebody off must come before off.

studyTips: Group phrasal verbs by intention: continue (carry on), progress (get on), discourage (put off), or criticise (tell off).
Practise object position aloud: finish the report off / finish it off; tell the workers off / tell them off.
Compare get on with a colleague and get on with your work; label each as relationship or task.
Create two short situations for put off: postpone a meeting versus discourage a visitor; notice the object changes.

exercises.prompt: The musician briefly stopped to adjust her microphone, then ___ singing.
exercises.feedback: Carried on singing means she resumed and continued an existing activity.

exercises.prompt: Despite a few disagreements, the two interns ___ well with one another.
exercises.feedback: Get on well with somebody refers to a good relationship.

exercises.prompt: The hotel charged us three times the advertised rate. We were ___.
exercises.feedback: Were ripped off describes being unfairly charged or cheated.

exercises.prompt: The emergency bell ___ during the rehearsal, so everyone left the hall.
exercises.feedback: An alarm goes off when it sounds; it does not mean it was switched off.

exercises.prompt: We paused for questions, then ___ the discussion. (carry on with / past simple; write the full verb phrase)
exercises.feedback: Carry on with a noun means continue a named activity; carried is the past form.

exercises.prompt: The children ___ arguing about whose turn it was. (keep on / past simple; write the full verb phrase)
exercises.feedback: Kept on arguing expresses an action that continued persistently.

exercises.prompt: After checking her messages, Leila decided to ___ her homework. (get on with; write the exact phrase)
exercises.feedback: Get on with + a task describes continuing or resuming it.

exercises.prompt: The head teacher ___ for running through the laboratory. (tell the pupils off; past simple; write the full verb phrase)
exercises.feedback: Tell somebody off for + -ing names a reprimand. The past-tense phrase is told the pupils off.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Even after the audience left, the actor carried on to practise.
acceptedAnswers: Even after the audience left, the actor carried on practising.
exercises.feedback: Carry on doing uses an -ing form to describe continuing an activity.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I get on really well my colleagues.
acceptedAnswers: I get on really well with my colleagues.
exercises.feedback: Get on well with somebody requires the preposition with.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: That disappointing review put off her buying the laptop.
acceptedAnswers: That disappointing review put her off buying the laptop.
exercises.feedback: Put somebody off doing places the person object before off.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The instructor told off them for arriving late.
acceptedAnswers: The instructor told them off for arriving late.
exercises.feedback: Tell somebody off is separable, so the pronoun them precedes off.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend stopped writing briefly but then continued. Say one past-tense sentence beginning "She" and ending "writing". Use carry on.
speakingExercises.feedback: Carried on writing means she continued the existing activity.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks whether Ravi and Kim have a good relationship. Reply with one sentence using these facts: Ravi and Kim / get on well / with each other. Use the present simple.
acceptedAnswers: Ravi and Kim get on well with each other.
speakingExercises.feedback: Get on well with each other describes a positive interpersonal relationship.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make one sentence from these facts: The alarm / go off / at midnight. Use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The alarm went off at midnight.
speakingExercises.feedback: Went off means that the alarm sounded.

speakingExercises.prompt: A break has ended. Tell your team in one sentence that you must resume the project now. Begin "We must" and use get on with.
acceptedAnswers: We must get on with the project now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Get on with the project means resume work on it.

speakingExercises.prompt: Paraphrase "The costly tickets discouraged us from attending" using these words: The costly tickets / put / us / off / attending. Use past simple.
acceptedAnswers: The costly tickets put us off attending.
speakingExercises.feedback: Put us off attending expresses that the price removed our willingness to go.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the pronoun position and say the full sentence, changing nothing else: "The teacher told off him for shouting."
acceptedAnswers: The teacher told him off for shouting.
speakingExercises.feedback: The object pronoun him must appear between told and off.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences using these facts: I / almost / doze off / during the film; my sister / keep on / talking. Use the past simple in both sentences.
acceptedAnswers: I almost dozed off during the film. My sister kept on talking.
speakingExercises.feedback: Almost dozed off means nearly fell asleep; kept on talking describes speech that continued.

speakingExercises.prompt: You painted most of a mural yesterday and completed the last small section this morning. Say one sentence beginning "I" and using finish it off in the past simple, ending with "this morning".
acceptedAnswers: I finished it off this morning.
speakingExercises.feedback: Finished it off means completed the remaining part of a task. The pronoun comes before off.

listeningExercises.audioText: We stopped the tour for a short rest, but the guide carried on explaining the route afterwards.
listeningExercises.prompt: What did the guide do after the break?
listeningExercises.feedback: Carried on explaining means the guide continued after the short interruption.

listeningExercises.audioText: I like my new supervisor. We get on well, even when the office is busy.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker say about the supervisor?
listeningExercises.feedback: Get on well indicates a positive relationship, not speed or employment status.

listeningExercises.audioText: After the interruption, we got on with the training session.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word phrasal expression immediately after "we".
listeningExercises.feedback: Got on with indicates resuming a named task.

listeningExercises.audioText: The staff alarm went off at dawn, but there was no emergency.
listeningExercises.feedback: Went off refers to the sounding of an alarm.

listeningExercises.audioText: I considered joining the club, but the membership fee put me off.
listeningExercises.prompt: Why did the speaker decide against joining?
listeningExercises.feedback: Put me off means the fee discouraged the speaker from joining.

listeningExercises.audioText: During the presentation, the intern kept showing off his technical knowledge instead of answering questions.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the intern trying to do?
listeningExercises.feedback: Showing off refers to trying to attract admiration or impress others.

listeningExercises.audioText: My uncle nearly dozed off on the return train.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word expression immediately after "nearly".
listeningExercises.feedback: Dozed off means began to fall asleep unintentionally.

listeningExercises.audioText: The manager told them off for ignoring the safety signs.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word phrase immediately after "manager".
listeningExercises.feedback: The person-object them goes between told and off.
